Between L=10L = 10L=10 and L=12L = 12L=12, the depth of the blocked circuit increases from 10 to 25 in the cz basis (from eight to 23 with fractional gates), and then stays the same up to L=50L = 50L=50. The fold increases the depth once, not once per strip. The drawing for L=50L = 50L=50 has four folds and eight stretched links, and the depth is the same as at L=12L = 12L=12, which has one fold. The depth stays the same because the depth penalties of all folds occur in parallel.

Result of the comparison. Beyond the width of the QPU, blocked order loses its depth advantage. At L=50L = 50L=50, both orderings reach 25 in the cz basis. The best interleaved seed reaches 22 between L=12L = 12L=12 and L=40L = 40L=40, but its median is 23 to 25. With fractional gates, blocked order (23) is deeper than interleaved order (19). Blocked order still has a lower gate count: 462 compared with 838 in the cz basis (45% fewer) and 412 compared with 592 with fractional gates (30% fewer), at the cost of one more qubit. Fewer gates can mean less accumulated error on a real device, which can be a reason to prefer blocked order on a QPU with a ladder. The observable that you measure at the end of the circuit can also affect the choice of encoding.

On Heron, which has no ladder, blocked order is much worse. Its best depth grows from 29 at L=4L = 4L=4 to 95 at L=50L = 50L=50 in the cz basis (92 with fractional gates), and the median and worst seeds at L=50L = 50L=50 give 134 and 166.

7. Beyond one dimension

All of the previous sections are one-dimensional, where the hardware needs to hold only a path or a ladder. A square lattice of sites is the case where the square connectivity of Nighthawk matters most, so this section briefly examines it. To keep the section short, it omits spin and uses the spinless model of the Simulate 2D Fermi-Hubbard dynamics with flow sets guide (Gandon et al., arXiv:2512.11418). That model has hopping and interaction on every nearest-neighbor bond of an R×CR \times CR×C lattice.

In the Verstraete-Cirac encoding of the model, every site gets its own ancilla (N=RCN = RCN=RC modes use 2N2N2N qubits), and the hopping splits into four flow sets (east, west, north, and south). A Clifford circuit of two-qubit depth 2, which acts on all rows or all columns at the same time, diagonalizes each flow set. As in 1D, the depth of the circuit therefore does not grow with the lattice. The guide shows each of these steps, but it does not transpile to a given connectivity. The following drawing shows how the model fits on Nighthawk.

The stripe layout on Nighthawk. Lattice row rrr runs down QPU column rrr as a stripe that alternates site, ancilla, site, ancilla (lattice column ccc is on QPU rows 2c2c2c and 2c+12c+12c+1). A site and its own ancilla are neighbors, an ancilla and the next site along the row are neighbors, and vertical neighbors are on adjacent QPU columns. Therefore, all hopping terms are on couplers, and the Clifford circuits need no routing. The interaction between two sites of the same row is not native, because the two sites are two QPU qubits apart, with the ancilla between them (the red arcs). These pairs are the same ZZ\texttt{ZZ}ZZ-type pairs that you routed in 1D, with one rzz gate per horizontal bond, so the routing cost is similar to the cost in 1D. The largest lattice that fits this layout is 10×610 \times 610×6 (60 sites, which use all 120 qubits).

draw_stripes([(3, 3), (10, 6)])

These results lead to the following high-level takeaways:

  • On Nighthawk, use blocked order with two ancillas. While the ladder fits on the QPU, its depth is half the depth of interleaved order (10 compared with 22 in the cz basis at L=10L = 10L=10). After the fold, its depth stays at 25 (23 with fractional gates). Interleaved order has an equally constant depth in the cz basis and a lower depth with fractional gates (25 and 19 at L=50L = 50L=50). Therefore, at large sizes, interleaved order has a small advantage in depth. The blocked circuit still needs far fewer two-qubit gates: 462 compared with 838 in the cz basis (about 45% fewer), and 412 compared with 592 with fractional gates (about 30% fewer), at the cost of one more qubit. Fewer gates can mean less accumulated error on a real device, which can be a reason to prefer blocked order.
  • Without square connectivity, use interleaved order. One ancilla and any path through the device give a constant depth on Heron too (25 in the cz basis and 19 with fractional gates at L=50L = 50L=50). On Heron, the blocked variant has no ladder to use. Its best depth grows with LLL (95 and 92 at L=50L = 50L=50, and 166 and 161 for the worst routing seed), and fractional gates barely reduce it.
  • Fractional gates lower the constant depth. Where the depth is constant, it drops from 25 to 19 for both interleaved variants and from 25 to 23 for blocked order on Nighthawk. At L=10L = 10L=10, the depth of the blocked circuit drops from 10 to 8. The gate counts also drop.
  • The ordering is a hardware decision, not a physics decision. Blocked and interleaved order are the same Hamiltonian with renamed modes, as the relabeling check in section 2 shows. The ordering changes which modes are neighbors, and the encoding and the coupling map see that change.
  • The structure is useful only with a synthesis that uses it. With a term-by-term synthesis (LieTrotter), the depth on a line grows linearly, to 599 at L=50L = 50L=50, compared with 23 for the flow-set circuit.
  • All results in this tutorial use custom syntheses. Both circuits use a one-Clifford recipe for every flow set, so the comparison is fair, but a different synthesis might change the numbers. Future releases of qiskit-fermions might automatically find a short-depth diagonalizing Clifford circuit.

Caveats. The depths are for noise-free coupling maps (FakeFez and FakeNighthawk), manually built fractional targets, and manually chosen layouts. The best of 20 routing seeds is an optimistic result by design. It is the depth that you can reach if you route a circuit many times and keep the best result, which is inexpensive to do before a run. The median is the result of a single transpilation, and it is never smaller than the best result. This tutorial compares structure, not fidelity. On Heron, the two-ancilla blocked variant is routed without a manual layout, because the heavy-hex lattice has no ladder. A better placement might do somewhat better than the router, but the lattice still has no ladder.
